clue.text: Calm air is such a disguise for this parlour game

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so the letters before it appear rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; the surface hides it as a linking word

explanation.surface: A party guest describes a calm atmosphere as the perfect cover for some indoor game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such' looks like part of the phrase 'such a disguise', but its letters belong in the mix too.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the familiar party game where players race for seats when the music stops.

clue.text: Mother a barrier to a dilettante Japanese girl

blocks.note: M is a standard abbreviation for mother
taken as written
a dam is a barrier holding back water
a butterfly flits from one interest to the next, like a dabbler

explanation.surface: A mother stands in the way of a frivolous young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Puccini's opera is Cio-Cio-San, a young geisha from Nagasaki who marries an American officer.

clue.text: Takes in a term of childish abuse

blocks.note: first meaning: draws in, absorbs, as through a straw
second meaning: the playground jeer '... to you!'

explanation.surface: Someone swallows an insult hurled like a schoolchild's taunt.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means drawing liquid inward by mouth, and the same word is a schoolyard jeer expressing contempt.

clue.text: Doing business in 'Change, perhaps, in the City

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the word given is only one possible arrangement of its letters
one element sits inside the other, as the clue says it is in it

blocks.note: 'Change is the old short form of Exchange, taken as written
a shop that is open is doing business

explanation.surface: Trading on the Exchange in the City of London, the financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the City of London and its Stock Exchange, but the city wanted is a foreign capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Danish capital is one instance of a large town, not the London financial district the surface suggests.

clue.text: At which business with shotgun can be regretfully reviewed?

definitions.text: At which business with shotgun can be regretfully reviewed?

blocks.clueFragment: At which business with shotgun can be regretfully reviewed?
blocks.note: surface reading: a gun dealer or hunter looking back on a shooting trip
setter's reading: a shotgun wedding, and the proverb 'marry in haste, repent at ...' names the time for regret

explanation.surface: Someone looks back with regret on an incident involving a shotgun.
explanation.walkthrough: A shotgun wedding is one forced by pregnancy; the proverb says those who marry in haste repent at this.
explanation.definitionFit: Free time is when there is no hurry, the opposite of the haste in the proverb about hasty marriage.

clue.text: He took new heart when he invaded Kent

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for new
the gist is the heart or core of a matter

explanation.surface: A warrior regains his courage as he lands in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England, said to have been conquered by the Jutish leader with his brother Horsa in the fifth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend makes this Jutish chieftain the leader of the first Germanic invasion and settlement of Kent.

clue.text: Turn over at 4

blocks.note: first meaning: run slowly in neutral, as an engine ticks over
second meaning: the answer to 4-down follows 'at', and being at that is having nothing to do

explanation.walkthrough: The 4 is a cross-reference to 4-down, so read the clue with that answer in place of the number.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine running unloaded is said to be ticking over, and a person with free time and no work is unoccupied.

clue.text: Where players have “their exits and their entrances”?

definitions.text: Where players have “their exits and their entrances”?

blocks.clueFragment: Where players have “their exits and their entrances”?
blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation from As You Like It about life as a play, where all men are players
setter's reading: actors literally coming and going from a theatre by their own back entrance

explanation.surface: Jaques's speech in As You Like It: all the world's a stage, and its people merely players.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors come and go through the backstage entrance at the theatre, separate from the public doors.

clue.text: Grammatical device frequent in Hansard

blocks.note: surface reading: indirect speech, the grammatical form 'he said that he would ...'
setter's reading: Hansard is the official record of Parliament's debates, so its whole content is speeches written down

explanation.surface: A grammar point is said to crop up often in the parliamentary record.
explanation.walkthrough: Hansard is the printed transcript of debates in the British Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Indirect speech is the grammatical term, and Hansard literally consists of speeches that have been reported.

clue.text: Cede point, confused by faint sound

indicators.note: something confused is muddled, so the letters are jumbled out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone concedes an argument, bewildered by a barely audible noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faint sound' means a word that sounds like faint: feint, a sham attack in fencing or boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: A feint is a trick move meant to mislead an opponent, which is a kind of trickery.

clue.text: Summer's too short for Shakespeare

blocks.note: surface reading: a complaint that the season does not last long enough
setter's reading: Sonnet 18 says that summer's ... 'hath all too short a date', the missing word being a term of tenancy

explanation.surface: A grumble that the warm season ends too soon, put in Shakespeare's mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: In the sonnet the word means a fixed period of tenure, like a rental agreement that runs out.

clue.text: Filial claim that carries strong force

blocks.note: the claim 'me' is a child saying 'it is me'
a son is the filial party

explanation.surface: A child's claim to be someone's offspring carries great weight.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Filial claim' as a child crying 'me, son', claiming kinship.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics this particle was proposed by Yukawa to transmit the strong nuclear force binding protons and neutrons.

clue.text: One of the sacred oracles, Hebrew but bordering on the universal

definitions.text: One of the sacred oracles, Hebrew

indicators.note: one thing placed on another comes after it, so the piece before this word is sent second

blocks.note: U is the film certificate meaning suitable for universal viewing
a rim is a border or edge

explanation.surface: A Hebrew oracle is described as close to universal in its reach.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film classification for universal audiences.
explanation.definitionFit: Urim and Thummim were objects in the Hebrew high priest's breastplate used to divine God's will.

clue.text: Refuse to allow a free vote

indicators.note: letters set free can move about and settle in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone blocks a proposal for an open ballot.
explanation.definitionFit: To block or forbid a proposal is the verb sense of the word used for a president's or council member's power to reject.

clue.text: Publicity man with note on swindle is on the march

blocks.note: a PRO is a public relations officer
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
a sting is a confidence trick

explanation.surface: A spin doctor caught up in a fraud is sent marching off.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'note on swindle' puts the note above the swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: Demonstrators who march through the streets with banners are objecting publicly to something.

clue.text: Draw attention to oneself, riding in front of the coach

blocks.note: a jockey who is riding is said to be up
a stage is short for stagecoach

explanation.surface: A rider shows off by galloping ahead of the coach.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who moves upstage forces others to turn away from the audience, stealing the limelight for themselves.

clue.text: A place for meditation in a food store?

blocks.note: first meaning, split into two words: a quiet chamber
second meaning: a room in a big house for preserves, cordials and cakes

explanation.surface: Someone seeks a quiet corner for contemplation inside a grocery shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is a silent chamber; as one, the old household larder where preserves and liqueurs were kept.

clue.text: Expel a number of people, say

blocks.note: first meaning: throw someone out of a place
second meaning: the attendance at an event or election

explanation.surface: Throwing out a crowd of people.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means eject, and the noun names how many people attended a meeting or voted in an election.

clue.text: Become weak, get nurse round for the final stage

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, wrapping one part about the other

blocks.note: to tend is to nurse or look after
to ail is to be unwell or weaken

explanation.surface: Someone growing frail calls in a nurse as life draws to a close.
explanation.definitionFit: The last part or closing portion of anything, such as a queue or a procession, is its extreme rear.

clue.text: The noise level is going to be lied about, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps marks the letters as one possible version, open to rearrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
C stands for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: Someone warns that the official noise figures will be misreported.
explanation.definitionFit: This logarithmic unit is how the loudness of sound is measured, so it stands for a measure of noise.

clue.text: Scratched, so got new dressing?

blocks.note: first meaning: withdrawn from a race or contest
second meaning: tire is an old word for attire, so this is dressed again

explanation.surface: Someone grazed themselves and so needed a fresh bandage.
explanation.definitionFit: A scratched runner has pulled out of the event; split as re-tired, it means given fresh clothes, tire being archaic for attire.

clue.text: Soldier again in the TA?

blocks.note: first meaning: serve once more
second meaning: the TA, or Territorial Army

explanation.surface: Someone returns to military service as a part-time territorial.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA was the Territorial Army, Britain's force of part-time volunteer soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A part-time soldier in the Territorial Army is a backup to the regular forces; split, the word means to serve a second time.

clue.text: List of food

blocks.note: first meaning: a register of names, as in an electoral register
second meaning: a small loaf of bread

explanation.surface: A menu or catalogue of things to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A register of names is called by the same word as a small individual bread bun.

clue.text: Book variety turns

blocks.note: first meaning: the ... of the Apostles, a book of the New Testament
second meaning: separate performances in a variety show

explanation.surface: An agent reserves some music-hall performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' reads as a verb, to reserve, but it is a noun naming a book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifth book of the New Testament has this name, and each performer's spot in a variety bill is one.

clue.text: To drink outside, find a basin

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: to sup is to drink
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone goes outdoors for a drink and looks for a bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone vessel for holy water near a church door is a kind of shallow bowl.

clue.text: Subject of a Sultan is soon in a rising

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: 'in a mo', short for in a moment, means soon

explanation.surface: A sultan's subject is about to join an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a rising' looks like a revolt, but 'in a' is just a link word here.
explanation.definitionFit: Oman is ruled by a sultan, so a citizen of that Gulf state is his subject.

clue.text: Mass producer (and, briefly, his distribution method?)

indicators.note: briefly asks for the phrase in a shortened, abbreviated form

blocks.note: goods sent by lorry go by road

explanation.surface: A manufacturer of goods in bulk, and how he gets them to market.
explanation.walkthrough: RD is the usual abbreviation of road. 'Mass producer' suggests a factory, but means a composer of Masses.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudor composer William Byrd wrote settings of the Latin Mass for the Catholic liturgy.

clue.text: Crazy as a diver?

blocks.note: first meaning: mad
second meaning: like a loon, the bird known in Britain as a diver

explanation.surface: Someone wonders if diving makes a person mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The loon of North America is called a diver in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means mad, and read as loon plus -y it means like that water bird.

clue.text: It is put up to stop ungentlemanly fellow interrupting dramatist

definitions.text: It is put up to stop

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something

blocks.note: J. M. Barrie was the dramatist who wrote Peter Pan
a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably

explanation.surface: A rude man heckles a playwright, so something is built to keep him back.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrier hastily erected across a street to block an advancing force is the classic obstruction.

clue.text: In which Chaucer wrote of wicket taking spin

blocks.note: a batsman at the wicket taking guard may ask for middle, lining up the bat on the middle stump
in American pool and billiards, english is side spin put on the ball

explanation.surface: Chaucer is pictured writing about a bowler taking wickets with spin.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the batsman taking guard asks the umpire for a line such as middle stump.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in the form of the language used in England from about 1100 to 1500.
